## Why this matters {.unnumbered}

*Draft.* Two paragraphs on what changes in residency: you will be handed a tool
that produces references, and you will be the one who signs whatever those
references support.

## The idea

*Draft.* The claim this chapter tests: a citation from a language model is a
prediction of what a citation looks like, not a lookup. When a group of medical
questions was put to a general chatbot, most of the references it produced did not
exist [@pmid:40206627; @pmid:37499282]. Tools that index the literature directly
behave differently — one head-to-head scored zero fabrications for a retrieval-based
tool against double-digit rates for general models [@pmid:42232526]. The rate is
not a constant; it is a property of the tool and the month.

The second half of the idea is that the same skepticism applies to the *evidence
about* AI. Regulatory clearance is not evidence of clinical benefit
[@pmid:33820998], and a randomized trial of physicians with model access found no
improvement in diagnostic reasoning over physicians without it, while the model
alone outperformed both [@pmid:39466245]. The published number is the optimistic
one.

## Do

### Part A — The fabrication hunt

*Draft.* Ask a general chatbot for five references on a clinical question in
**your specialty**, then score each 2/1/0 against PubMed using the scoring key in
@sec-check. Search recipe:

```
("large language model" OR "artificial intelligence") AND <your specialty>
AND (validation OR "external validation")
```

Filter to the last three years and choose one review-style question from what you
find.

### Part B — Grading the evidence

*Draft.* Ten claims about ambient documentation, each with its source. Grade the
study design behind each, then compare the pre/post pilots with the multi-system
cohort [@pmid:41920565].
